g-khankids: A free, ad-free, subscription-free learning app for preschoolers aged 2-7 that parents love for its generosity, but which rests on a fragile technical base and hits a ceiling of difficulty.
g-lifesum: A mature calorie tracker that ran on trust in precise manual logging and a clean diary, now wedging a mandatory AI layer between the user and the log — breaking the exact daily-logging reflex its multi-year habit was built on.
g-loop: An ascetic open-source habit tracker that beats paid rivals through radical simplicity and zero ads, yet the same minimalist philosophy turns away anyone who needs sync, grouping, or serious numeric-habit tracking.
g-loseit: A mature calorie tracker with a huge food database and fast logging that keeps people on multi-year streaks — but the habit it builds rests on a fragile foundation of barcode scanning, fitness-tracker sync, and database accuracy, and every wobble in those pillars threatens to send users to a rival.
g-mathkids: A free math game for preschoolers and early-grade kids built around the character Lucas: parents are won over by the «no ads, no subscription» promise but frustrated that the hints hand over the answer and the child learns to tap, not to count.
g-monefy: Monefy wins on radically frictionless expense entry — one screen, one tap, a pie chart — but the same minimalist data model hits a ceiling the moment a user wants per-category budgets, month-to-month carry-over, or any real analytics.
g-moneylover: A mature personal-finance tracker built on multi-currency wallets, budgets and shared access that kept loyal users for years through frictionless manual entry — but whose core value, trust in the balance and sync, is now undermined by a redesign and a broken web side.
g-moneymanager: A disciplined manual double-entry tracker for people who want to count every cent themselves: it wins on simplicity and a decade of loyalty, but loses everyone who expects SMS auto-capture and seamless cross-device sync.
g-mstodo: A free cross-platform to-do list grown out of Wunderlist and wired into the Microsoft 365 ecosystem: it rests on instant phone-to-PC sync and a home-screen widget, while its hidden pain is that tying it to a corporate Microsoft account turns your personal list into a hostage of your employer.
g-myfitnesspal: The default calorie diary that wins on a giant food database and habit power, but its 2026 redesign broke the one thing it did best — the at-a-glance day — and moved once-free basics behind a subscription.
g-mynetdiary: A mature calorie tracker that wins on an unusually generous free core and has become the landing pad for MyFitnessPal refugees — yet that same generosity is undercut by aggressive upsells and creeping feature bloat.
g-noom: Noom is a behavioral weight-loss program built on psychology and micro-lessons that wins beginners through education and coaching, but loses serious calorie-counters with a weak food database and a pivot toward AI and GLP-1 sales.
g-notion: A desktop-grade «second brain» builder for people willing to learn, crammed into a mobile app that mostly just reads what you built on the big screen — and the entire pain lives in that gap.
g-obsidian: A local-first markdown engine for building a «second brain» that wins enthusiasts through file ownership and plugins, but loses the mass mobile user to a steep learning curve and a desktop-first mobile shell.
g-onenote: A free-canvas notebook for people living inside the Microsoft ecosystem who author on desktop and merely consult on the phone — the mobile build is deliberately trimmed to a viewer, and it is exactly there that trust collapses in a product whose one promised job is to keep the note safe.
g-pomodoro: A minimalist, ad-free Pomodoro timer that many users adore for its cleanliness — yet its one core job, signalling the end of an interval, regularly fails.
g-productive: A minimalist habit tracker that wins beginners with a clean interface and the don't-break-the-chain effect, yet loses those same users at the start: a hard free-habit cap hits the paywall before the product ever proves its value.
g-readingeggs: A strong literacy and math program for preschoolers and early-grade kids that children genuinely love, wrapped in a buggy app that keeps logging them out and dragging along an aggressive subscription.

g-sagomini: A collection of mini-games for toddlers loved by kids and the parents who grew up on it, but nearly all content now sits behind a monthly subscription — breaking the childhood-era promise of free play.
